c2.explanation: The only retrieved paper is a systematic review of functional foods in clinical trials. It lists flaxseed oil and grape seed oil among the foods reported to regulate inflammation, but it does not directly test whether eating seed oils in general, such as soybean, corn or sunflower oil, causes inflammation. None of the evidence tests the claim as stated.
limitations: The review covers functional foods broadly and does not focus on the omega-6-rich seed oils usually meant by 'seed oils'
The abstract only says these foods 'regulate' inflammation and gives no effect sizes or direction for each oil
No study looks at typical dietary seed-oil intake and inflammation markers

c3.explanation: A large US cohort (ev_37758268) linked more starch, added sugar, refined grains and starchy vegetables with more weight gain. In the same cohort, more carbs from whole grains, fruit and non-starchy vegetables went with less weight gain. A pooled Finnish cohort analysis (ev_37149710) found no link between total carbohydrate intake and weight gain, so the evidence suggests carb type matters, not carbs as a whole.
limitations: Both weight studies are observational and cannot show cause and effect
No randomised trials of carb intake vs. fat gain were retrieved
The claim is a blanket statement, while the evidence varies by carbohydrate type
The athletic-performance, mortality and diabetes papers do not address weight gain

c4.explanation: None of the retrieved papers directly compares diets with equal calories but different carb and fat content and measures fat gain. Most look at how carbohydrate affects athletic performance, or at mortality. One small trial found that pistachios led to more BMI loss than pretzels at similar calories, which hints that the food matters. But it is a single study of snack type, not a test of carbs versus fat versus calories.
limitations: Most papers are about sports performance, not body weight or fat gain
Pistachio RCT is small, tests one snack swap during calorie restriction, and only hints against the claim
No metabolic-ward trials or meta-analyses comparing equal-calorie diets with different carb and fat content were retrieved

c5.explanation: None of the retrieved papers looks at whether processed carbohydrates lead to overeating, energy intake or satiety. Most cover carbohydrates for athletic performance. The others cover carbohydrate intake and mortality, and carb counting for diabetes.
limitations: No studies on ultra-processed or refined carbohydrates and energy intake were retrieved
Most papers are about sports nutrition, a different topic
The mortality cohort study is observational and does not measure overeating

c6.explanation: None of the retrieved papers measures satiety, fullness or energy intake after eating high-fiber whole foods, so none tests whether such foods are harder to overeat. The reviews link fiber and whole grains to heart and metabolic health, gut microbiota and lower body weight. Those are associations, not tests of the satiety mechanism the claim describes.
limitations: No study measures satiety, appetite or ad libitum energy intake
The weight link in ev_23609775 is observational and does not show that fiber makes food more filling
Two papers are about dairy cattle nutrition and are not relevant
Several items are only titles or broad narrative reviews

c7.explanation: None of the retrieved papers tests whether carbohydrates are an essential nutrient. A large cohort meta-analysis (ev_30122560) linked both very low and very high carbohydrate intake with higher death rates, but this is only an association. A trial in triathletes (ev_39786965) found that a very-low-carbohydrate diet still sustained endurance performance. The rest are reviews of how athletes use carbohydrate as fuel; none addresses whether carbs are needed in the diet at all.
limitations: Most papers are about athletes' performance, not about whether people in general need carbs in their diet
The mortality evidence is observational and shows only an association, and the results depended on what replaced the carbohydrate
No reference source on nutrient requirements (for example, dietary reference intakes) was retrieved

c8.explanation: A large US cohort of 221,000 adults followed for up to 33 years found that people who ate the most butter had 15% higher total mortality and higher cancer mortality, while swapping butter for plant oils was linked to lower mortality. A review of 20 diet trials found that replacing butter with soft margarine improved blood lipids. Neither study suggests that eating more butter is healthy.
limitations: No study tests butter eaten specifically as a snack; the evidence covers butter intake in general.
The mortality evidence is observational: it shows an association, not cause.
The lipid review compares butter with margarine and measures blood lipids, a stand-in for health outcomes.
The other retrieved items are letters, off-topic papers or have no abstracts.

c9.explanation: None of the retrieved studies tests whether moderate saturated fat intake is safe, and none looks at active people with healthy lifestyles. A large Norwegian cohort linked higher saturated fat intake (median about 15% of calories) to higher death rates, and an overfeeding trial found saturated fat increased liver and visceral fat. A narrative review argues that the link between saturated fat and heart disease is weaker than often assumed. These findings are indirect and point in different directions, so they cannot confirm or refute the claim as stated.
limitations: No study defines or tests 'moderate' intake, or looks specifically at active or healthy-lifestyle people
The harm signals come from observational associations (cohort, cross-sectional, biomarker studies) or from overfeeding, not normal intake
The supportive material is a narrative review and opinion pieces, mostly about dairy and heart disease

c10.explanation: The claim doesn't say which nutrient it means or what counts as an "extreme" amount, so it can't be tested as stated. The one retrieved paper, a review of carbohydrate intake for athletes, recommends about 30–90 g per hour during long events. It does not look at whether intakes far beyond that are less than optimal or harmful.
limitations: The claim doesn't name the nutrient or define 'extreme', which leaves little to test
The only evidence is a narrative review of carbohydrate fuelling in athletes, which does not test very high intakes
Hedged wording ('probably not optimal') makes the claim hard to falsify

c11.explanation: The only paper retrieved is a 1997 narrative review of how alcohol affects the endocrine system. It does not look at fat gain, energy balance or calorie deficits, so nothing here tests whether hormonal problems can cause fat gain during a calorie deficit.
limitations: The only paper is off-topic: it covers alcohol's effects on hormones, not fat gain during a calorie deficit
No studies measure body fat or energy balance in people with endocrine disorders
It is a narrative review, and an old one (1997)

c12.explanation: Neither retrieved paper tests whether fat gain or loss is determined by calories eaten versus calories burned. One is a classroom laboratory exercise that teaches energy expenditure and fat oxidation and assumes the energy-balance principle. The other is a narrative review of adipocyte mitochondria that describes adipose tissue as central to energy balance but does not test the claim.
limitations: The lab exercise is a teaching activity that assumes energy balance; it does not test it in people
The mitochondria review is mechanistic and only indirectly related
No controlled feeding trials or authoritative reference on energy balance were retrieved

c13.explanation: Reviews of many human epidemiologic studies link higher vegetable and fruit intake with lower risk of several cancers, and the 1996 review also notes benefits for heart disease, stroke, diabetes and other conditions. A 2014 review found that most studies report cognitive benefits. None of the retrieved papers show that vegetables in general are harmful.
limitations: Most evidence is observational and narrative reviews; association does not prove cause
Studies often combine fruit and vegetables
The IARC-based review rates the evidence for cancer prevention as only limited
Several retrieved papers (microbiome, agriculture, consumer acceptance) do not address health effects

c14.explanation: The narrative review names plant compounds commonly called anti-nutrients, including oxalates, phytates and tannins, and examines whether they pose a real health threat. These are the compounds known to bind minerals, which fits the claim's modest wording that some vegetables contain compounds that "may" reduce mineral absorption.
limitations: Only one narrative review was retrieved, and only its abstract.
The abstract does not itself state that these compounds bind minerals or reduce their absorption.
The review questions how much these compounds matter for health, which the claim does not address.

c15.explanation: The claim doesn't say which food it means. None of the retrieved papers looks at whether eating a particular food gives a net gain in nutrients. They cover diet quality and thinking skills in older adults, how the body controls appetite, insect detoxification, lemur food preferences and obesity models, so none tests the claim either way.
limitations: The claim leaves out which food 'them' refers to, so there is nothing specific to test
All retrieved papers are off-topic or indirect (animal studies, studies of appetite mechanisms, broad diet-quality studies)
No paper weighs the nutrients a food provides against any nutrient losses or anti-nutrient effects

c16.explanation: The claim doesn't say which food it means. The retrieved reviews and lab studies show that many plant foods (oats, millets, seaweed, grape pomace, cereal grains) provide fibre and antioxidant or anti-inflammatory polyphenols. None of them tests whether one particular food provides phytochemicals that other foods can't. If anything, finding similar compounds in many different foods makes "can't get from other foods" seem doubtful. But no paper directly tests that point.
limitations: Claim does not identify the food in question
Papers are narrative reviews and lab/compositional studies, not tests of uniqueness
Only one paper describes a compound unique to one food (avenanthramides in oats), and the claim's food is unknown
Antioxidant/anti-inflammatory activity mostly shown in vitro

c17.explanation: None of the retrieved papers tests dietary diversity, meaning eating many different types of food, as a factor in health. The diet review (ev_37867396) links healthy dietary patterns, such as plant-based and Mediterranean diets, with longer life, and the fibre review (ev_36786062) links fibre to lower disease risk. Neither one looks at food variety itself, and the other three papers are about forests, fish and moths.
limitations: No study measures dietary diversity or food variety scores against health outcomes
The diet and fibre reviews are narrative reviews of observational cohort studies, and they address diet quality or fibre, not variety
Three of the retrieved papers have nothing to do with nutrition
